name: Ethinylestradiol for hair

lead: Ethinylestradiol (EE) is a synthetic estrogen taken by mouth, best known as the estrogen component of most combined oral contraceptives. In women with androgen-related hair thinning, clinicians sometimes use estrogen-containing pills, often combined with an anti-androgen, with the aim of reducing androgen effects on the scalp.

The appearance goal is better hair density or slower loss. Published evidence on EE specifically for hair is limited, and this page focuses on documenting what the drug is and how it is discussed rather than on any course of use.

paras: It is prescribed by a clinician, usually as a combined pill that also contains a progestin or an anti-androgen such as cyproterone acetate. Hair effects, where they occur, are generally described as gradual over months, and use is typically alongside other hair-loss approaches.

EE is prescription-only in most countries. Documented risks include venous blood clots, cardiovascular events, liver effects and, at higher doses, greater clot risk; it is contraindicated in people with a history of clots and certain other conditions. Common effects include breast tenderness, headache, nausea and fluid retention.

chain: Androgen effects on scalp are reduced
Slower thinning or modest density gain over months
angle.text: When prescribed for androgen-related hair thinning, ethinylestradiol works hormonally rather than on the follicle directly. The aim is to hold or improve scalp density, usually as part of a broader plan with a prescriber.

lead: Ethinylestradiol is a synthetic estrogen derived from estradiol, developed in the 1930s and introduced for medical use in 1943.[1] It is absorbed well when taken by mouth and became the estrogen in nearly all combined oral contraceptives from the 1960s.[1]

Its link to hair comes through hormones: pills containing it are used by some prescribers for hair thinning linked to androgens in women, either alone or with an anti-androgen. The goal is to reduce androgen activity at the scalp and support density.
Estrogen-containing pills are generally prescription-only.[1] A general reference on the drug does not list hair loss among its established uses.[1]

paras: Combined pills containing EE are among the hormonal options clinicians consider for female patients whose hair thinning is androgen-driven. The effect is indirect, through hormone balance.
EE is used mainly for contraception and menopausal symptoms, and has also been used in hypogonadism and osteoporosis prevention.[1]

Common effects include breast tenderness, headache, fluid retention, nausea and dizziness. Rarer serious risks include blood clots, cardiovascular events and liver damage, with clot risk rising at higher doses.[1] It is contraindicated with a history of clots and certain other conditions.[1]
EE is prescription-only in most places.[1] It is not an approved hair-loss treatment, so hair use is off-label.

timeline.event: Begins appearing in combined birth control pills.[1]
